_meta.name: obs-095 business viability rubric
_meta.purpose: Single source of truth for the OBS-SPEC-095 scorer. The calibration harness and the production scorer MUST both read this file (spec 5.3) — otherwise calibration validates a scorer that is not the one shipped.

scale.warning: The API returns an EXPECTED LEVEL, so a perfect score is 4.0, not 5.0. Off-by-one here silently shifts every dimension down one.

_meta.direction_warning: Every dimension is named so that HIGHER IS MORE FAVOURABLE. 'Competitive pressure' was renamed 'Competitive room' because the original name invites an inverted score — a scorer reading 'pressure' as high-when-bad would invert one dimension against the other four and the composite would be meaningless.

gates._note: Floors are on the 1-5 display scale. 1 means failing, so every floor is >= 2. A floor of 1 cannot fire.

market_headroom.instructions: Judge ONLY market headroom: is there room for a new or small entrant to be chosen in this category at all? Ignore how good this particular business is, ignore its brand, and ignore how differentiated it is. Consider whether the category the business names is a real category a buyer would recognise, whether it is growing or shrinking, and whether new entrants do get chosen in it. A category can be large and still be a trap if the label is contested or the buyer does not shop that way.
levels: No headroom. The category named is a trap — contested, or an artefact of how the business describes itself — and there is no identifiable category in which a buyer could choose them.
Very little. The category is real but shrinking, or so broad the business cannot be placed within it.
Moderate. A real category with real buyers, but flat, or structurally unfavourable to new entrants.
Good. A real, growing category in which new entrants do visibly get chosen.
Strong. A large, growing category with documented, growing demand and plenty of room for new entrants.

competitive_room.instructions: Judge ONLY competitive room: how much space does competition leave for this business to operate and earn? Higher means MORE room — a fragmented, uncontested market. Lower means less room — concentrated incumbents, price-driven commoditisation, or a floor price set by a much larger player. Assess concentration, the strength of the named competitors, and whether the market competes primarily on price. Do not consider the business's own positioning or quality.
levels: No room. Dominated by concentrated incumbents, competing almost entirely on price, with no viable margin left.
Very little. A dominant player or a severe price floor; the business is structurally squeezed.
Some. Crowded and price-contested, but gaps exist for a small operator.
Good. Competitive but fragmented; several players coexist without a single dominant one crushing the rest.
Strong. Uncontested, fragmented, with no dominant player and no established price floor.

position_availability.instructions: Judge ONLY position availability: is the position the business wants to occupy still OPEN, or does someone already own it? Higher means more open. Assess whether the word or idea the business claims is already owned by a named competitor in the buyer's mind, and whether the claim is one that competitors could trivially copy or already share. A claim that several competitors also make is NOT an available position. Consider what the business actually claims, as stated.
levels: Taken and defended. The claimed position is clearly owned by an established competitor.
Mostly taken. The claim is shared by several competitors, or copyable in a season.
Partly open. The claim is not owned outright, but it is not exclusively theirs either.
Open. The position is genuinely unoccupied, with only weak or incidental overlap.
Wide open. The position is clearly unoccupied and the incumbents are not even oriented toward it.

defensibility.instructions: Judge ONLY defensibility: is what makes this business different hard for a competitor to copy, and hard to build? Higher means more defensible. Consider each claimed differentiator: could a competitor buy the same ingredient, hire the same supplier, or copy the same message this quarter? A differentiator that rests on a purchasable input, a public document, or a price point is NOT defensible. A differentiator that rests on accumulated trust, an owned distribution channel, a proprietary dataset, or years of relationship is defensible. Consider the business as described, including anything it says about itself.
levels: Nothing to defend. There is no differentiator at all, or the one claimed is freely purchasable by any competitor.
Fragile. The differentiator exists on paper but a competitor can copy it in weeks.
Moderate. Some durable element exists — a relationship, a channel, or a track record — but it is thin or unproven.
Strong. A real durable element that would take a competitor a year or more to replicate.
Very strong. Multiple compounding advantages that a well-funded competitor could not replicate quickly.

demand_reach.instructions: Judge ONLY demand reach: is there an identifiable, reachable group of buyers who would pay for this, and can this business find them? Higher means more reachable. Consider whether the customer is described in a way that identifies a real group with a trigger to buy, whether that group is concentrated somewhere the business can reach it, and whether it is willing to pay the stated price. A demographic such as an age band is NOT a reachable segment on its own. Do not consider whether the market is large.
levels: No identifiable buyer. The customer is undefined, or defined so broadly no one can be targeted.
Weak. Only a demographic is named; no trigger, no channel, and no evidence they will pay this price.
Moderate. A describable segment with a plausible trigger, but no established route to reach them.
Good. A clearly identified segment with a trigger and at least one credible channel to reach it.
Strong. A tightly defined, concentrated, paying segment that the business can reach directly and cheaply.

input_sufficiency.instructions: Judge ONLY whether the submitted information contains enough to assess this business's position. You need enough to identify its category, something that could constitute a differentiator or positioning, some sense of its competitors, and some sense of its customer. If one of those is entirely absent, or the answers are placeholders or generic filler with no specific content about this business, the input is insufficient.

criteria.sufficient: There is enough specific, substantive information to assess the category, the claimed differentiator, the competitors and the customer.
criteria.insufficient: At least one of category, differentiator, competitors or customer is absent, or the answers are placeholders or generic statements that could apply to any business.
